kakekotoba.reading_primary: いつ見き (when did I see [it/you])
kakekotoba.reading_secondary: 泉 (izumi, embedded via sound echo with いづみ river name)
kakekotoba.interaction: The phrase いつ見きとてか plays on the sound of 泉 (Izumi) from the preceding ku — 'itsu miki' echoes 'Izumi', binding the river name to the rhetorical question 'when did I ever see you' that drives the poem's logic of unexplained longing.

jokotoba.text: みかの原わきてながるる泉川
jokotoba.pivot: 泉川 (Izumigawa) / いつ (via sound-association いづみ→いつ)
jokotoba.function: The entire kami-no-ku describes the Izumi River flowing forth distinctly through Mika Plain; this serves as an extended preface whose function is purely to generate, through sound-association between 'Izumi' (泉) and 'itsu' (いつ, 'when'), the phrase いつ見き that opens the shimo-no-ku, rather than contributing literal narrative content about the speaker's feelings.

honkadori.source_poem: Man'yōshū-style river-naming poems referencing Mika no Hara and the Izumi River (Yamashiro province)
honkadori.echoed_phrase: みかの原わきてながるる泉川
honkadori.function: Invokes the established place-name imagery of Mika Plain and the Izumi River as a conventional utamakura, lending the poem geographic and literary resonance while setting up the sound-pivot into いつ

kigo.note: Izumi River is a famous utamakura (place name) in Yamashiro province, prized for its clear, cold spring-fed waters; it carries no strict seasonal marker but is conventionally associated with the purity and coldness of flowing water, sometimes linked to autumn/winter imagery of clear streams in classical poetry. No other lexical item (mika no hara as plain, wakite as verb of dividing/springing forth, nagaruru as flowing) carries seasonal weight; this poem is essentially a love poem (koi) using a river-name jokotoba rather than a seasonal poem, so no true kigo governs it.

bipartite.kami_theme: The Izumi River flows forth distinctly (wakite) through Mika Plain — a pure topographical image of a river dividing and running clear.
bipartite.shimo_theme: The speaker wonders, bewildered, when he ever actually saw her, that he should feel such longing (koishikaruran) — an unexplained, seemingly causeless love.
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku functions as jokotoba whose sole purpose is to generate, through the homophonic echo of Izumi (泉) with itsu (いつ, 'when'), the rhetorical question that opens the shimo-no-ku. The river's flowing has no causal or metaphorical bearing on the emotion itself — the connection is purely acoustic/associative, making this a sound-driven pivot rather than an image-based one (hence 'other' rather than simile-implicit or seasonal-pivot).
